messages.content: Our camp has 500 people. How much water do we need per day and how many collection points?

Given:
- Population: 500 people
- Standard: UNHCR/Sphere minimum 15–20 L/person/day
- Maximum walking distance to water point: 500m (Sphere standard)

Formula / rule:
- Total daily water = 500 × 15 = 7,500 L minimum; 500 × 20 = 10,000 L target
- Water point capacity: each handpump or tap serves ~250 people at 15 L/person
- Number of points = population ÷ 250 = 2 minimum
- Queue time target: no person waits more than 15–30 minutes
- Distribution rate: 1 L/min per tap × 8 hours operation = 480 L/tap/day
- Taps needed: 10,000 ÷ 480 = 21 tap-hours → 3 taps running 7 hours each

Result:
- Minimum: 2 water points, 3 taps total
- Target: 4 water points distributed so no one walks more than 500m
- Daily supply needed: 7,500–10,000 L

Safety note:
- Separate water points for drinking/cooking vs. bathing/laundry — cross-contamination kills
- Priority queue for pregnant women, elderly, children under 5 — dehydration kills them first
- Track crude mortality rate — rising diarrhea deaths = water system failing

If uncertain / escalate:
- If water per capita drops below 7 L/day = crisis threshold — prioritize drinking/cooking only, suspend other uses
How do you set up a latrine system for a camp of 1,000 people from scratch?

Given:
- Population: 1,000 people
- Context: emergency camp, no existing sanitation
- Goal: prevent diarrheal disease outbreak

Formula / rule:
- Sphere standard: maximum 20 people per toilet in emergency (50 absolute maximum)
- Minimum: 1,000 ÷ 20 = 50 latrines
- Separate by gender: 60% female, 40% male (women need more time, higher vulnerability)
- Defecation field (emergency day 1): mark clearly, 30m from water sources, 50m from dwellings
- Pit latrine depth: 1.5–2m, 1m above groundwater table minimum
- Slab: raised, self-draining, fly-proof cover
- Distance rules: >50m from water source, <50m from shelter (balance access vs. contamination)
- Handwashing station: 1 per 10 latrines, ash or soap mandatory

Result:
- Day 1: demarcate open defecation field immediately — stops random contamination
- Week 1: construct 25 emergency pit latrines (Sphere temporary minimum)
- Week 2–4: complete 50 latrines with slabs and handwashing stations

Safety note:
- Women's latrines must have lockable doors and lighting — GBV risk is highest at sanitation points
- Children under 5 produce most fecal pathogens — install child-friendly steps or child latrines
- Flies move from latrine to food in minutes — cover pits, cover food
- Cholera can spread entire camp within 48 hours if one contamination event reaches water supply

If uncertain / escalate:
- Diarrhea in >5% of camp within 24 hours = suspected outbreak — isolate, treat, report immediately
We need to distribute food to 2,000 people fairly. What is the system and how many calories per person?

Given:
- Population: 2,000 people
- Goal: equitable distribution, prevent hoarding and exclusion
- Standard: UNHCR general ration = 2,100 kcal/person/day

Formula / rule:
- Total daily calories: 2,000 × 2,100 = 4,200,000 kcal/day
- Typical ration composition: cereals (60%), pulses (20%), oil (10%), CSB/fortified blend (8%), salt (2%)
- Cereals: ~3,500 kcal/kg — need ~400g/person/day of cereal
- Pulses: ~3,400 kcal/kg — need ~60g/person/day
- Oil: ~9,000 kcal/kg — need ~25g/person/day
- Total dry weight per person: ~500g/day = 1 tonne/day for 2,000 people
- Distribution system: household ration card → family size recorded → ration per family collected weekly
- Distribution point throughput: 1 team processes ~200 families/hour
- 2,000 people ÷ 5 avg family size = 400 families → 2 hours with 1 team

Result:
- Weekly distribution: 3.5 kg cereal + 420g pulses + 175g oil + per person
- 2 distribution points, 1 distribution day per week, 2 teams = manageable
- Issue ration cards with photo ID if possible — prevents double registration

Safety note:
- Women should receive ration cards, not male household head — evidence shows food reaches children when women control it
- Separate queue for elderly, disabled, pregnant/lactating women — vulnerability weighting
- Children under 5 and pregnant women need supplementary feeding: CSB porridge, Plumpy'Nut
- Monitor mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) weekly for children — MUAC < 115mm = severe acute malnutrition emergency

If uncertain / escalate:
- If rations run below 1,500 kcal/person/day for more than 3 days, mortality spikes — escalate to WFP immediately
Can a small community build a gravity-fed water system from a hillside spring without pumps?

Given:
- Water source: hillside spring
- Goal: gravity-fed distribution to village below
- No pumps, no electricity

Formula / rule:
- Pressure head: P = ρ × g × H (H = height difference between spring and tap)
- At H = 10m: P = 1000 × 9.81 × 10 = 98,100 Pa ≈ 1 bar (adequate for tap flow)
- Minimum head for functional tap: 5m (0.5 bar)
- Pipe sizing: flow rate Q = A × v (A = pipe cross-section, v = velocity)
- PVC pipe 1 inch (25mm): carries ~0.3 L/s at 1 m/s velocity
- For 200 people × 20 L/day = 4,000 L/day ÷ 28,800 seconds (8hr) = 0.14 L/s needed → 1-inch pipe sufficient
- Spring box: concrete chamber around spring eye, sealed, overflow pipe, covered
- Distribution: spring box → storage tank at high point → gravity to taps below

Result:
- System components: spring box + 2,000L storage tank + PVC pipe + 3–4 tap stands
- Build time with community labor: 2–3 weeks
- Cost: primarily pipe and cement — often under $500 materials for 200-person system
- No ongoing energy cost — gravity runs it forever

Safety note:
- Spring box must be fenced — animal contamination destroys entire system
- Overflow pipe prevents pressure buildup and spring flooding
- First flush each morning contains overnight bacterial growth — let run 30 seconds before collection
- Uphill latrines = catastrophic contamination risk — site latrines downhill and downslope from spring

If uncertain / escalate:
- Test spring yield in dry season — some springs disappear; size storage tank for 3-day reserve
What causes cholera to spread so fast in camps and how do you stop an outbreak in 48 hours?

Given:
- Pathogen: Vibrio cholerae
- Setting: refugee camp, dense population
- Goal: contain outbreak within 48 hours

Formula / rule:
- Transmission route: fecal-oral only — contaminated water or food, not air
- Infectious dose: as low as 1,000 CFU (colony forming units) — extremely low threshold
- Incubation: 2 hours to 5 days — fast onset means rapid case explosion
- R0 in uncontrolled camp setting: 2–5 (each case infects 2–5 others)
- Fatality rate untreated: 25–50%; with ORS: <1%
- Critical interventions in order:
  1. Hour 0–6: identify cases, establish Oral Rehydration Corner (ORC)
  2. Hour 6–12: chlorinate entire water supply to 0.5 mg/L FRC minimum
  3. Hour 12–24: case isolation area (Cholera Treatment Unit), cohorting
  4. Hour 24–48: trace water source contamination, hyperchlorinate suspected point
  5. Ongoing: 0.2–0.5 mg/L FRC at all taps, soap at all latrines
- ORS production: 10L batches, correct ratio, distributed free
- Severely dehydrated cases: IV Ringer's Lactate 100mL/kg over 3 hours

Result:
- 80% of deaths prevented by ORS alone — the treatment is water + salt + sugar
- Water chlorination stops transmission within one incubation cycle (5 days)
- Isolation prevents healthcare worker exposure and secondary spread

Safety note:
- Do NOT close the camp — movement disperses cases to new populations
- Dead bodies are NOT primary transmission risk in cholera — focus on living patients
- Community messaging critical: shame and fear cause people to hide cases — announce treatment works

If uncertain / escalate:
- Cases doubling every 24 hours despite intervention = water source not identified — test all sources, consider tanker delivery only
How do you design a solar microgrid for a village of 300 people with no grid connection?

Given:
- Population: 300 people (~60 households)
- Load estimate: 5 LED lights + phone charging + radio per household
- No grid connection
- Goal: reliable evening lighting minimum

Formula / rule:
- Load per household: 5 × 5W LEDs × 5hrs + 10W phone × 2hrs + 5W radio × 3hrs = 125 + 20 + 15 = 160 Wh/day
- Total village load: 60 × 160 = 9,600 Wh/day = 9.6 kWh/day
- Add 20% system losses: 9.6 × 1.2 = 11.5 kWh/day needed from panels
- Peak sun hours (tropical): 4.5 hrs/day
- Panel array needed: 11,500 Wh ÷ 4.5 hrs = 2,556W peak → 13× 200W panels
- Battery bank: 2 days autonomy × 9.6 kWh × 2 (50% DOD) = 38.4 kWh
- At 48V system: 38,400 Wh ÷ 48V = 800 Ah battery bank
- Charge controller: MPPT type, sized for 2,600W panel input at 48V
- Distribution: low voltage DC (48V) for short distances, or single-phase AC with inverter for larger village

Result:
- System size: 2.6 kW panels, 38 kWh battery bank, 3kW inverter
- Cost estimate: $4,000–8,000 USD at current panel prices
- Managed by village energy committee — metered connections, small monthly fee funds maintenance

Safety note:
- DC systems at 48V: shock risk is low but wire sizing critical — undersized wire = fire
- Battery bank: ventilated room, no open flames, check electrolyte monthly for lead-acid
- Overload protection: fuses at each household connection
- Community buy-in essential — without maintenance committee, system fails within 2 years regardless of quality

If uncertain / escalate:
- If village has mobile phone shop or small mill: size up by 50% — productive use loads drive economic sustainability of entire system
What is the most dangerous failure mode when setting up a refugee camp and how do you prevent it?

Given:
- Context: rapid-onset refugee camp setup
- Goal: identify highest-mortality failure and prevent it

Formula / rule:
- Historical mortality data (UNHCR): biggest killers in first 30 days are diarrheal disease, measles, pneumonia, malaria — not violence
- Most dangerous single failure: water source contamination combined with high population density
- Cascade sequence:
  1. Inadequate latrine coverage (>50 people/latrine)
  2. Open defecation near water source
  3. Fecal contamination of drinking water
  4. Diarrhea outbreak → dehydration → deaths, especially children under 5
  5. Camp overwhelmed → other systems fail → mortality spike
- Secondary failure: invisible populations
  - Unaccompanied children not registered
  - Disabled persons cannot reach water/food distribution
  - Women avoiding latrines due to safety → open defecation → contamination loop
- Crude mortality rate (CMR) baseline: <1/10,000/day
- Emergency threshold: >1/10,000/day = crisis
- Double emergency: >2/10,000/day = catastrophic, requires immediate external escalation

Result:
- Prevention priority order:
  1. Water: clean source or treatment from day 1
  2. Latrines: at least 1 per 50 people within 48 hours
  3. Registration: count everyone, including invisible groups
  4. Measles vaccination within 72 hours for all children 6 months–15 years
  5. Daily CMR monitoring — the number that tells you if the system is working

Safety note:
- Coordination failure = duplicate aid in one sector, zero in another = people die in the gap
- Assign sector leads on day 1: water lead, health lead, protection lead — one person accountable per sector
- Never assume another agency covered something — verify with daily coordination meeting

If uncertain / escalate:
- CMR rising despite interventions = surveillance gap — go door to door, something is being missed
How do photonic crystals enable thermophotovoltaic systems and could this power a remote village?

Given:
- Technology: thermophotovoltaic (TPV) with photonic crystal emitters
- Source material: MIT 2.997 lectures on selective thermal emission
- Application: remote village power generation

Formula / rule:
- Standard TPV problem: hot emitter at 1500K radiates broadband spectrum; PV cell only absorbs photons above bandgap (Eg)
- Wasted photons below Eg: transmitted as heat, not electricity
- Photonic crystal solution: 2D tungsten photonic crystal with periodic holes (radius r, lattice d) creates photonic bandgap
- Result: emitter radiates only above PV cell's Eg → spectral efficiency jumps from ~40% to ~93%
- System efficiency: TPV + PhC emitter → practical 20–30% overall conversion
- Heat source options: concentrated solar, biomass combustion, propane, waste heat from cooking
- Biomass TPV: wood/agricultural waste → combustion at 1200–1500K → PhC emitter → GaSb PV cell → electricity
- 1 kg dry wood combustion: ~15 MJ heat → at 20% TPV efficiency → 3 MJ = 833 Wh electricity

Result:
- Yes, viable for remote village with biomass fuel
- Advantages over solar PV: 24/7 operation, no batteries needed, fuel storable
- Disadvantages: requires precision nanofabricated photonic crystal emitter — not field-manufacturable yet
- Current status: lab-demonstrated, micro-TPV generators at 1–5W commercially available (propane-powered)
- Village-scale TPV: 5–10 year horizon for cost-competitive systems

Safety note:
- Emitter temperatures (1200–1500K) require refractory materials — tungsten, silicon carbide only
- Biomass combustion: CO and particulate emissions require ventilation — indoor use kills
- GaSb PV cells: contain antimony — disposal requires hazardous waste handling

If uncertain / escalate:
- For immediate village power: solar PV + battery is proven and deployable today — TPV is the upgrade path when biomass is abundant and solar is unreliable
How would you design a community composting and biogas system that also handles human waste safely?

Given:
- Community: 100–500 people
- Goal: integrate waste → biogas → fertilizer loop
- Inputs: food waste, agricultural waste, potentially fecal sludge

Formula / rule:
- System design: co-digestion of organic waste types
- Carbon:Nitrogen ratio target: 25:1 for optimal methane production
  - Food scraps: C:N ~15:1 (nitrogen-heavy)
  - Straw/leaves: C:N ~60:1 (carbon-heavy)
  - Human feces: C:N ~8:1 (very nitrogen-heavy)
  - Mix: 2 parts straw + 1 part food waste + 1 part feces → ~25:1
- Retention time: 30–40 days at 25–35°C
- Gas yield: 0.3–0.5 m³ biogas per kg volatile solids
- Community digester for 100 people: ~50kg waste/day → 15–25 m³ biogas/day
- 25 m³ biogas = ~12 hours cooking fuel for community kitchen
- Pathogen destruction: fecal sludge requires minimum 30 days retention at 35°C to reduce helminths
- OR thermophilic digestion at 55°C: 5–7 days sufficient for full pathogen kill
- Effluent (digestate): excellent fertilizer — nitrogen retained, pathogens reduced
- Digestate safety: test for helminth eggs < 1 per gram before agricultural use

Result:
- Integrated loop: waste → 40-day digester → biogas for cooking + digestate for crops
- Community kitchen powered by own waste stream
- Fertilizer eliminates need to purchase chemical inputs
- Closes the nutrient loop: soil → food → human → waste → soil

Safety note:
- Never use fresh feces directly on food crops — 1-year composting or verified pathogen kill required
- Biogas pipe connections: use soap bubble test monthly for leaks — methane accumulation is explosion risk
- Digester overflow in rainy season: design overflow channel directed away from water sources
- Community must understand and operate system — technical dependency without local ownership = system collapse

If uncertain / escalate:
- If digestate smells of ammonia: C:N ratio too low, add more carbon material immediately — nutrient loss and system acidification risk
What is the Carnot efficiency limit and why does it matter for building power systems in the field?

Given:
- Concept: Carnot efficiency — maximum theoretical efficiency of any heat engine
- Context: field power systems using fire, solar thermal, biogas

Formula / rule:
- Carnot efficiency: η = 1 − (T_cold / T_hot) where temperatures in Kelvin
- Example 1: campfire (T_hot = 800°C = 1073K), ambient (T_cold = 30°C = 303K)
  - η = 1 − (303/1073) = 71.8% theoretical maximum
  - Real engine achieves 20–35% of theoretical → actual ~15–25%
- Example 2: solar thermal trough (T_hot = 400°C = 673K), ambient (T_cold = 303K)
  - η = 1 − (303/673) = 55% theoretical → real ~18–22%
- Example 3: wood gasifier + steam engine (T_hot = 600K), ambient (303K)
  - η = 1 − (303/600) = 49.5% → real ~12–18%
- Key insight: HIGHER temperature difference = higher efficiency ceiling
- Every degree of cold-side cooling matters: dropping T_cold by 20°C increases Carnot efficiency
- Concentration solar thermal: raises T_hot → raises efficiency → why parabolic dishes outperform flat panels for power

Result:
- No field engine exceeds Carnot limit — physics enforces this
- Practical rule: if T_hot < 200°C, don't bother with heat engine for electricity — use thermoelectric or direct PV instead
- If T_hot > 400°C (focused solar, biogas flame): Stirling engine or steam engine viable
- Maximize ΔT: insulate hot side, cool cold side with water or airflow

Safety note:
- Steam engines: pressure vessels require relief valves — no exceptions. Boiler explosions are catastrophic.
- High-temperature systems: radiant burns at 400°C+ require full shielding
- Wood gasifier: produces CO as intermediate — lethal in enclosed spaces

If uncertain / escalate:
- If efficiency seems far below expectation: measure actual temperatures, not assumed — field conditions often cut T_hot by 30–40% vs. design
How do you build a community seed bank to ensure food security across multiple disaster seasons?

Given:
- Goal: maintain viable seed supply through repeated disasters
- Context: rural/agricultural community, flood/drought cycles

Formula / rule:
- Seed viability physics: seed longevity doubles for every 1% reduction in moisture content and every 5°C reduction in temperature (Harrington's rule)
- Target storage conditions: moisture content < 8%, temperature < 15°C
- Without refrigeration: dry seeds in sun until hard (crack test), store in airtight container with desiccant
- Moisture test: bite seed — should crack cleanly, not bend
- Container options: sealed glass jars > sealed metal tins > sealed plastic bottles (in order of preference)
- Desiccant: silica gel (recharge by heating at 120°C for 2 hours) or wood ash (absorbs moisture)
- Seed quantity: store minimum 3× planting quantity — one for planting, one for loss, one emergency reserve
- Rotation: use oldest seeds first, replace annually with fresh harvest
- Genetic diversity: store minimum 5–10 varieties per crop — monocultures vulnerable to single disease
- Location: elevated, waterproof, separate from food stores (prevent eating seed stock in famine)

Result:
- Simple system: dried seeds in sealed glass jars with silica gel, stored in coolest available room
- Community governance: 3-person seed committee with written inventory, distributed copies
- Annual community seed fair: exchange varieties, prevent inbreeding, maintain diversity

Safety note:
- Never store all seeds in one location — distribute across 3 households minimum
- Label everything: crop name, variety, harvest date, planting rate — unlabeled seeds get wasted
- Germination test before planting season: sprout 10 seeds on wet cloth — if fewer than 7 sprout, seed stock compromised
- Hybrid seeds (F1) do NOT breed true — save only open-pollinated/heirloom varieties for seed banking

If uncertain / escalate:
- If entire seed stock fails: contact UNHCR/FAO emergency seed distribution — do not plant untested seeds in desperation without germination check
What is the physics of why molten salt thermal storage works and could a community build one?

Given:
- Technology: molten salt thermal energy storage (TES)
- Source: MIT 2.997 solar concentration lectures
- Goal: assess community-scale feasibility

Formula / rule:
- Thermal storage principle: sensible heat storage — Q = m × Cp × ΔT
  - Q = energy stored (J)
  - m = mass of salt (kg)
  - Cp = specific heat capacity of molten salt (~1,500 J/kg·K)
  - ΔT = temperature swing (°C)
- Commercial system: solar salt (60% NaNO₃ + 40% KNO₃)
  - Melting point: 220°C (liquid above this)
  - Operating range: 290°C (cold tank) to 565°C (hot tank)
  - ΔT = 275°C → 1 tonne salt stores: 1000 × 1500 × 275 = 412 MJ = 114 kWh
  - Cost: ~$10–15/kWh of storage (vs. $150–300/kWh for lithium batteries)
- Community-scale: 10 kWh storage → 88 kg salt → very achievable mass
- Heat source: concentrated solar (parabolic trough or dish), wood combustion
- Heat extraction: heat exchanger → steam → Stirling engine or thermoelectric

Result:
- Physics: YES, community scale is viable for thermal storage
- Barrier: operating temperature requires 290°C+ — above water boiling, requires pressurized or non-water heat transfer fluid
- Simpler community alternative: phase change materials (PCM) at lower temperatures
  - Paraffin wax: stores/releases heat at 50–60°C — useful for food warming, space heating, NOT electricity
  - Salt hydrates: CaCl₂·6H₂O melts at 29°C, stores 190 kJ/kg — passive cooling/heating possible

Safety note:
- Molten nitrate salts at 400°C+: contact with organic material causes fire — strict contamination protocols
- Freeze risk: if system loses heat below 220°C, salt solidifies in pipes — system destroyed
- Community systems should target PCM or water-based storage below 100°C for safety

If uncertain / escalate:
- For community electricity storage: lithium batteries or lead-acid remain safer and simpler despite cost — molten salt is utility-scale technology for now
How do you build a community FM radio transmitter to broadcast emergency information when all phones and internet are down?

Given:
- Context: disaster, no internet or mobile network
- Goal: broadcast emergency information via FM radio
- Receiver availability: most communities have battery/hand-crank FM radios

Formula / rule:
- FM frequency band: 87.5–108 MHz
- Low-power FM transmitter (legal limit in most countries without license): 100mW EIRP → ~1–5 km range
- Emergency powers in most jurisdictions allow unlicensed operation in declared disaster zones
- Transmitter construction: simple FM oscillator circuit (NE555 or dedicated FM IC like BH1415)
- Antenna: half-wave dipole for FM = 300/frequency(MHz) / 2 meters
  - At 100 MHz: antenna length = 300/100/2 = 1.5m each arm
- Power: 9–12V DC → runs from car battery or small solar panel
- Range improvement: height matters most — each doubling of antenna height increases range ~40%
  - Antenna at 10m height: 2–5 km range
  - Antenna at 30m height: 5–15 km range
- Modulation: standard FM mono sufficient for voice broadcast

Result:
- Buildable from salvaged electronics or low-cost kit (~$10–30 in parts)
- Power consumption: 1–5W total → runs days on car battery
- Broadcast schedule: fixed times (7am, 12pm, 6pm) so population knows when to listen
- Content priority: water/food distribution locations, medical points, missing persons, security

Safety note:
- Avoid broadcasting on frequencies used by aviation (108–137 MHz) — illegal and dangerous
- Identify transmitter at start of each broadcast: prevents panic about unknown signal source
- High antenna = lightning target — include lightning rod and ground wire
- Do not broadcast unverified information — misinformation in disaster kills (wrong evacuation routes, false all-clears)

If uncertain / escalate:
- If range insufficient: relay stations using two radios (receive + rebroadcast on different frequency) extend coverage across terrain obstacles
What would a fully self-sufficient village energy system look like combining solar, biogas, micro-hydro, and wind?

Given:
- Village: 500 people, rural, no grid
- Goal: 100% renewable, resilient energy system
- Resources: solar, flowing stream, agricultural waste, seasonal wind

Formula / rule:
- Load analysis first:
  - Lighting: 500 people × 20Wh/day = 10 kWh/day
  - Cooking: 500 × 2,000 kcal/day thermal = ~2.3 kWh electricity equivalent (biogas better for cooking)
  - Productive use (mill, pump, phone, radio): ~5 kWh/day
  - Total electricity: ~15 kWh/day
  - Cooking fuel: ~25 m³ biogas/day (separate system)

- Source sizing:
  1. Solar PV (primary): 4 kWp array → 18 kWh/day at 4.5 peak sun hours → covers all electricity
  2. Micro-hydro (baseload if stream available): 500W continuous → 12 kWh/day → reduces battery dependency dramatically
  3. Biogas (cooking fuel only): 10–15 m³/day from 300-person waste → 60% of cooking fuel
  4. Wind (supplementary): 1–2 kW turbine where wind >4 m/s average → 5–10 kWh/day additional

- Storage:
  - With micro-hydro: batteries sized for solar-only nights = 20 kWh
  - Without micro-hydro: batteries sized for 2-day autonomy = 30 kWh

- System resilience:
  - Single source failure: micro-hydro covers cloudy periods; biogas covers cooking when solar panels damaged
  - Diversification = resilience — no single point of failure

Result:
- Achievable today with proven technology
- Cost: $15,000–40,000 USD depending on site (amortized over 20+ years = $750–2,000/year)
- Per capita: $30–80/person/year vs. $200–500/person/year for diesel generation
- Managed by community energy cooperative — revenue from productive use (milling fees) funds maintenance

Safety note:
- Integration complexity: multiple sources need coordinated charge controllers and load management
- Simplest integration: DC bus at 48V, all sources input through appropriate controllers
- Community technical training non-negotiable — 2-week training minimum for 3 village technicians
- Spare parts inventory: fuses, charge controllers, inverter — remote location means 6-month supply on hand

If uncertain / escalate:
- If budget constrained: micro-hydro first (if stream available) — continuous power, no storage needed, lowest maintenance. Solar second. Biogas third for cooking.
How does a Stirling engine work and why is it useful for off-grid power generation from biomass?

Given:
- Engine type: Stirling (external combustion)
- Fuel: biomass (wood, agricultural waste, biogas)
- Goal: understand suitability for off-grid electricity

Formula / rule:
- Operating principle: sealed gas (air, helium, hydrogen) cyclically heated and cooled between hot and cold chambers
  - Hot side: combustion heats gas → expands → pushes piston → mechanical work
  - Regenerator: porous metal matrix stores heat between cycles (key efficiency component)
  - Cold side: gas cools → contracts → cycle repeats
- Carnot efficiency applies: η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot
  - At T_hot = 650°C (923K), T_cold = 50°C (323K): η_Carnot = 65%
  - Real Stirling engines achieve 30–40% of Carnot → practical 20–26%
- Key advantages over steam engines for field use:
  - No high-pressure steam — no boiler explosion risk
  - External combustion — burns anything (wood, dung, biogas, solar heat)
  - Quiet operation
  - Long service life (no internal combustion fouling)
- Size range: 1W (microgeneration) to 100kW (utility)
- Common field sizes: 1–25 kW for community applications
- Dish/Stirling concentrating solar: parabolic dish focuses sun → 700°C+ focal point → Stirling engine → 30% solar-to-electric efficiency (highest of any solar technology)

Result:
- Ideal for biomass-rich, sun-poor communities (forest areas, rainy climates)
- 25 kW unit: burns ~10–15 kg wood/hour → powers 300-person village lighting
- Combined heat and power (CHP): waste heat from cold side heats water → 80% total energy utilization

Safety note:
- Working gas hydrogen (highest efficiency): flammable, requires sealed system integrity checks
- Air-charged Stirling: safer, less efficient — preferred for field deployment
- Hot side reaches 600–700°C — fire hazard near flammable materials
- Flywheel stores mechanical energy — entrapment hazard, install guard

If uncertain / escalate:
- Stirling engines require precision manufacturing — not field-fabricatable. Source from supplier, train local technician for maintenance only.
How do you design a passive cooling system for food storage in a hot climate without electricity?

Given:
- Climate: hot, arid or tropical
- Goal: extend food shelf life without refrigeration
- Method: passive evaporative cooling

Formula / rule:
- Evaporative cooling physics: Q = m × L_v
  - L_v (latent heat of vaporization of water): 2,257 kJ/kg
  - Each gram of water evaporated removes 2.26 kJ from the surroundings
- Pot-in-pot cooler (Zeer pot):
  - Inner clay pot + outer clay pot + wet sand between them
  - Water evaporates from outer pot surface → cools inner space
  - Temperature drop achievable: 15–25°C below ambient in dry climates
  - At 40°C ambient, 20% humidity: inner temperature reaches ~15–25°C
  - At 40°C ambient, 80% humidity (tropical): only 5–8°C drop — much less effective
- Wind exposure amplifies evaporation: place in ventilated shade, oriented to prevailing wind
- Daily maintenance: add ~2L water to sand each morning
- Shelf life extension: tomatoes 3 days → 3 weeks; peppers 1 day → 2 weeks; leafy greens 1 day → 5 days

Result:
- Best application: arid/semi-arid climates where humidity < 50%
- Materials: two clay pots, sand, water, cloth cover
- Cost: near zero if clay pots locally available
- Alternative (tropical/humid): underground storage at 0.5–1m depth maintains ~18–22°C year-round regardless of humidity

Safety note:
- Zeer pot does NOT reach refrigeration temperatures — does not stop all bacterial growth
- Meat and dairy: still high risk even in Zeer pot — consume within 24 hours
- Underground storage: inspect for rodents and insects — use sealed containers inside the pit
- Clay pot must remain unglazed — glazed pots don't allow water evaporation through walls

If uncertain / escalate:
- If humidity consistently > 70%: abandon Zeer pot approach, use fermentation and salt curing for preservation instead — evaporative cooling won't work meaningfully
What is the minimum viable community health post and what training do health workers need to save the most lives?

Given:
- Context: disaster/remote setting, no hospital within reach
- Goal: define minimum viable health infrastructure and training
- Population served: 500–2,000 people

Formula / rule:
- Biggest killers addressable at community level (UNHCR data):
  1. Diarrheal disease → ORS, zinc, water treatment education
  2. Acute respiratory infection (pneumonia) → amoxicillin, pulse oximeter, referral
  3. Malaria → rapid diagnostic test (RDT), artemisinin combination therapy (ACT)
  4. Malnutrition → MUAC measurement, Plumpy'Nut, therapeutic feeding referral
  5. Obstetric emergency → clean delivery kit, active management third stage labor, emergency referral
  6. Wound infection → irrigation, debridement, amoxicillin/metronidazole

- Minimum supply kit per 1,000 population/month:
  - ORS sachets: 500
  - Zinc tablets: 200 courses
  - Amoxicillin 500mg: 300 courses
  - ACT malaria treatment: 50 courses
  - Plumpy'Nut: 50 cartons
  - RDT malaria: 100 tests
  - Clean delivery kits: 10
  - Oral rehydration salts: 20 kg bulk

- Community Health Worker (CHW) training minimum: 5 days covering:
  - Danger signs requiring referral (cannot treat at community level)
  - ORS preparation and administration
  - MUAC measurement and malnutrition classification
  - Malaria RDT and treatment protocol
  - Wound irrigation technique
  - Clean delivery support

- CHW ratio: 1 per 100–200 households

Result:
- Minimum viable post: 1 room, 1 trained CHW per 500 people, above supply kit
- This setup prevents majority of preventable deaths without physician
- Referral pathway: document nearest functional health facility, distance, transport options — before emergency occurs

Safety note:
- CHWs must know their limits — the most important skill is recognizing what they cannot treat
- Danger signs always refer immediately: convulsions, unconsciousness, inability to drink, severe respiratory distress, postpartum hemorrhage
- Antibiotic stewardship: use only for confirmed bacterial infection — overuse creates resistance that kills future patients
- Record keeping: patient register mandatory — surveillance catches outbreak before it explodes

If uncertain / escalate:
- Any suspected outbreak (3+ similar cases): report to district health office within 24 hours regardless of communication difficulty — use any available channel
